title: The Branch
text:
At the tip of the pine a bird
sings, arrested,
trembling above its trill.


It rises, an arrow, on the branch,
vanishes among wings
and pours itself out in music.


The bird is a splinter
that sings and burns alive
inside a yellow note.


I lift my eyes: there is nothing.
Silence upon the branch,
upon the broken branch.
editorial_note: The song’s metamorphoses—bird, arrow, splinter, flame, yellow note—are kept swift and physical; the repeated branch closes on the silence left by flight.

title: Mystery
text:
The air shines, shines,

midday shines,

but I do not see the sun.


And from presence to presence

everything turns transparent to me,

but I do not see the sun.


Lost among transparencies,

I go from reflection to radiance,

but I do not see the sun.


And it strips itself bare in the light

and questions every splendor,

but does not see the sun.
editorial_note: The final él is rendered as it, preserving the uncertainty between sun, light, and perceiving self; repetition makes visibility itself the obstruction.

text:

The bird is a splinter

that sings and burns alive

inside a yellow note.


I lift my eyes: there is nothing.

Silence upon the branch,

upon the broken branch.
editorial_note: This separately sourced witness of “The Branch” uses the same reviewed language while preserving its expanded line spacing and first-line title.

title: Facing the Sea
text:
1


Has the wave no form?

In one instant it sculpts itself

and in another crumbles

into the one that rises, round.

Its movement is its form.


2


The waves withdraw

—haunches, backs, napes—

but the waves return

—breasts, mouths, foam—.


3


The sea is dying of thirst.

It writhes, with no one,

in its bed of rocks.

It dies of thirst for air.
editorial_note: The damaged source delimiters around the bodily lists are restored as dashes; wave-form becomes anatomy, then the sea’s impossible thirst for its elemental other.

title: Words
text:
Turn them over,
seize them by the tail (let them squeal, whores),
whip them,
give sugar to the balky ones’ mouths,
blow them up, balloons, prick them,
suck out their blood and marrow,
dry them,
geld them,
trample them, gallant rooster,
wring their necks, cook,
pluck them,
gut them, bull,
ox, drag them,
make them, poet,
make them swallow all their words.
editorial_note: The poem’s brutal imperative register and shifting animal metaphors are not softened; rejegas becomes balky ones, retaining the resistant mares within the feminized words.

editorial_note: This separately lineated witness of “Words” preserves the same reviewed imperatives and its first-line title.

title: Lightning at Rest
text:
Stretched out,

stone made of midday,

half-closed eyes where white shades into blue,

a half-open smile.

You rise halfway and shake your lion’s mane.

Then you lie down,

a slender groove of lava in the rock,

a sleeping bolt.

While you sleep I caress and polish you,

slender axe,

arrow with which I set the night on fire.


Far off the sea battles with swords and feathers.
editorial_note: The reclining beloved remains stone, lava, lightning, axe, and arrow in one continuous sculptural sequence; the distant sea answers with its own weapons and softness.

title: Two Bodies
text:
Two bodies face to face

are sometimes two waves

and the night is ocean.


Two bodies face to face

are sometimes two stones

and the night is desert.


Two bodies face to face

are sometimes roots

entwined in the night.


Two bodies face to face

are sometimes knives

and the night, lightning.


Two bodies face to face

are two falling stars

in an empty sky.
editorial_note: The incantatory syntax remains nearly literal so each transformation—water, stone, root, blade, star—alters both the lovers and the night around them.
